title: Add NetworkError and tighten retry logic
summary: Ky now wraps a fetch failure with a known network message in a typed `NetworkError`. By default it retries only `HTTPError`, `TimeoutError` and `NetworkError`, and throws every other error at once.

links.title: Issue #545: Best way to handle Fetch errors
sholladay: Ky retries all fetch errors
sholladay: wrap fetch errors in a NetworkError

steps.title: Fetch fails with a vague error
steps.body:
When a request cannot reach the server, `fetch` rejects with a plain `TypeError`. Each runtime writes its own message: "Failed to fetch" in Chrome, "fetch failed" in Node.js, "Load failed" in Safari 17 and later.

In issue #545, an app got these errors from time to time. The same request worked on the next attempt. The author asked how Ky can retry only network errors.

links.title: Issue #545: Best way to handle Fetch errors

steps.title: Ky retried every unknown error
steps.body:
Before this PR, `#calculateRetryDelay` retried almost every error of a retriable method, up to the retry limit. Only two errors stopped it: a `TimeoutError` when `retryOnTimeout` is false, and an `HTTPError` that the status rules reject.

So a network failure got a retry. A bug also got a retry, such as a `TypeError` from a custom `fetch` function. After the last attempt, the `beforeError` hooks and the caller got the raw `TypeError`.

links.title: sholladay: Ky retries all fetch errors

steps.title: Only the message shows a network error
steps.body:
A network failure has no error type of its own. It is a `TypeError`, like many bugs. Only the message tells the two apart, and the message is different in each runtime.

So Ky must keep a list of known messages. A runtime with a message that is not on the list gives a network error that Ky cannot find. In #545, sholladay named this cost. He preferred to retry an error when its message is unknown.

links.title: sholladay: wrap fetch errors in a NetworkError

steps.title: Retry only the errors that Ky knows
steps.body:
sindresorhus chose the strict rule, and called it the most pragmatic solution. His reason: new runtimes do not come often.

- Ky wraps a fetch failure with a known network message in a new `NetworkError`.
- By default, Ky retries only `HTTPError`, `NetworkError`, and `TimeoutError` when `retryOnTimeout` is true. It throws every other error at once.
- A network error with an unknown message is not retried. A `retry.shouldRetry` function that returns `true` can still retry it.

links.title: PR #842: Add NetworkError class and tighten retry logic

steps.title: What the PR changes in the code
steps.body:
- `#fetch` catches the error of the fetch call. When `isRawNetworkError` matches it, `#fetch` throws a `NetworkError` that keeps the original error in `cause`.
- `#calculateRetryDelay` throws each error that is not a `TimeoutError`, an `HTTPError` or a `NetworkError`.
- `isRawNetworkError` checks the raw `TypeError`. The new type guard `isNetworkError` checks for a `NetworkError`. They are two different functions.
- `isRawNetworkError` is a copy of the `is-network-error` package v1.3.1, so Ky still has no dependencies. In the review, sholladay found the copy odd, because Ky has a compile step. sindresorhus answered that a compile step for one dependency that seldom changes is not worth the effort.
- `NetworkError` extends `KyError`. Ky exports it with `isNetworkError`. The change shipped in v2.0.0.

steps.title: Ky in five facts
steps.body:
- Ky is a small HTTP client on top of `fetch`. App code calls it as `ky.get(url)` or `ky(url)`.
- Each call makes one `Ky` object in `Ky.create`. The call returns a promise of the `Response`.
- One call can send the request more than once. Each send is an attempt. `#fetch` makes one attempt.
- After a failed attempt, Ky decides: it waits and sends the request again, or it stops.
- When Ky stops, the promise rejects with the error. The app code gets the error in its `catch`.

steps.title: The errors of an attempt
steps.say: An attempt fails with an error. The type of the error tells Ky what went wrong.

terms.meaning: The base class of the errors that Ky creates. `isKyError` checks for it.
The `KyError` for a response with a status that is not 2xx. `error.response` holds the `Response`.
The `KyError` for a call that runs out of time. The default `timeout` is 10 s for all attempts of the call together.

The `TypeError` that `fetch` throws when no response arrives, such as for a DNS failure or a lost connection. Each runtime words its message in a different way, such as "Failed to fetch" in Chrome and "fetch failed" in Node.js.
New in this PR. The `KyError` that wraps a raw network error. `error.cause` holds the raw error.
Any other error of an attempt, such as a bug in a custom `fetch` function. It is not an `HTTPError`, a `TimeoutError` or a `NetworkError`.

steps.title: The retry decision
steps.say: After a failed attempt, Ky checks the error and the options. Then it retries or stops.

terms.meaning: An attempt after the first one. `#retryCount` counts the retries of one call.
The most retries for one call. The default is 2, so one call sends at most 3 attempts.
The HTTP methods that Ky retries: by default `get`, `put`, `head`, `delete`, `options` and `trace`. So by default Ky does not retry a `POST` or a `PATCH`.
The statuses of an `HTTPError` that Ky retries. The default list is 408, 413, 429, 500, 502, 503 and 504.
The check after each failed attempt. It throws the error to stop, or it returns the wait before the next retry.

An optional app function that runs in the retry decision, after the checks of the retry limit and the method. It returns `true` to retry, `false` to stop, or `undefined` to let Ky decide by the type of the error.
The option that lets the retry decision retry a `TimeoutError`. It is `false` by default, so a timeout stops the call.

steps.title: The wait and the hooks
steps.say: A retry waits first. Hooks let the app code act before a retry and before the final error.

terms.meaning: The wait before a retry, which doubles after each retry. By default, it is 300 ms before the first retry and 600 ms before the second.
App functions that run after the backoff, before each retry. They get the error and can change the request, return a `Response` instead, or stop the retries.
App functions that run once, just before Ky throws the final error to the app code. Each hook can return a different error to throw.

steps.title: Where retry errors come from
steps.say: Four types of Ky errors reach the retry decision. The PR adds `NetworkError`, the error for a failed connection.

notes.text: `#fetch` sends one attempt. By default, it calls `fetch` through the `timeout` helper. `fetch` is the runtime fetch, or the `fetch` option of the app.

When `fetch` rejects, the new `catch` in `#fetch` calls `isRawNetworkError`. A `TypeError` with a known runtime message, such as `Failed to fetch` in Chrome or `fetch failed` in Node.js, becomes a `NetworkError`. The original error is in its `cause`. Any other error passes unchanged.
When the time ends first, `timeout` aborts the fetch and rejects with a `TimeoutError`. The time limit is the `timeout` option (10 s by default), for all attempts together.
A response can also fail. With `throwHttpErrors` on (the default), `Ky.create` makes an `HTTPError` for a non-2xx status. An `afterResponse` hook that returns `ky.retry()` causes a `ForceRetryError`.
All these errors go to `#calculateRetryDelay`. It returns a delay to retry, or throws the error. `NetworkError`, `TimeoutError`, `HTTPError` and `ForceRetryError` all extend `KyError`.

steps.title: The order of the retry checks
steps.say: `#calculateRetryDelay` runs its checks in a fixed order. The first check that decides wins. The PR changes the end of the chain.

notes.text: Each failed attempt goes to `#calculateRetryDelay`. The retry limit comes first. `retry.limit` is 2 by default, so Ky makes at most 3 attempts. Then it throws the last error.
A `ForceRetryError` retries and skips all the checks below. Each retry waits first. The default backoff (`#calculateDelay`) waits 300 ms, then 600 ms.
Any other error needs a method in `retry.methods`: `get`, `put`, `head`, `delete`, `options` and `trace` by default. So by default, Ky does not retry a `POST`, except after `ky.retry()`.
When the app sets `shouldRetry`, a result of `true` or `false` decides. Any other result, such as `undefined`, goes on to the default checks.

A `TimeoutError` retries only when `retryOnTimeout` is on. It is off by default. An `HTTPError` retries only for a status in `retry.statusCodes`, such as 503. The PR gives both checks their own `return`.
New: a `NetworkError` retries, and every other error is thrown at once. Before the PR, the last line retried every error that passed the checks above, also an error from a bug in a custom `fetch`.

steps.title: Check
steps.question: An app calls `ky.post(url, {json})` with the default options, and the server refuses the connection. What does the app get?

options.why: `#fetch` wraps the error for every method. Then the method check throws it, because `post` is not in `retry.methods`.
A `NetworkError` retries only for a method in `retry.methods`, and the default list has no `post`.

options.text: The raw `TypeError` from `fetch`, after one attempt.
options.why: The `catch` in `#fetch` wraps the error before the retry decision runs, so the method does not matter.

steps.say: App code calls `ky.get(url)`, and the network fails. `#fetch` now turns the fetch failure into a `NetworkError`, and the retry decision retries it. In this run, the second attempt gets a response.

steps.title: Each attempt runs inside #retry
steps.say: Every attempt runs inside `#retry`. When an attempt throws, `#retryFromError` decides if a next attempt runs. The PR does not change this loop. It changes the errors that go into it.

notes.text: `ky.get` merges the instance defaults, the call options and the method. Then it calls `Ky.create`.
`Ky.create` passes `#fetch` to `#retry`. One call of `#fetch` is one attempt.
`#retry` awaits the attempt. When the attempt throws, `#retryFromError` gets the error. It returns the response of a later attempt, or it throws.

steps.title: A fetch failure becomes a NetworkError
steps.say: A network failure used to leave `#fetch` as the raw `TypeError` of the runtime. Now `#fetch` catches it and throws a `NetworkError`.

notes.text: Before, `#fetch` returned the fetch promise without `await`. A network failure reached `#retry` as the raw `TypeError`.
Now the attempt sits in a `try` block, and both returns use `await`. Without `await`, the promise rejects after the function has left the `try` block, and the `catch` does not see it.

`timeout` calls `options.fetch` with a timer for the time that is left. A fetch rejection goes to `reject` unchanged. When the timer fires first, `timeout` aborts the request and rejects with a `TimeoutError`.
The `catch` wraps a raw network error in a `NetworkError`, with the original error as `cause`. Every other error, such as a `TimeoutError`, leaves `#fetch` unchanged.
`NetworkError` is new. It extends `KyError`, like `HTTPError` and `TimeoutError`. Its message names the method and the URL, and `request` holds the request that failed.

steps.title: Only known network messages count
steps.say: Fetch rejects with a `TypeError` on a network failure, but a bug can throw a `TypeError` too. `isRawNetworkError` tells them apart by the message.

notes.text: `isRawNetworkError` is inlined from the `is-network-error` package, v1.3.1. It accepts only an `Error` object with the `name` `TypeError` and a string message.

Some runtimes need a pattern. Safari 17 says only `Load failed`, so that message counts only when the error has no stack or has the Sentry marker. Deno and Chrome can add the URL or the host name, so their messages match by the start.
Every other message must be in `errorMessages` exactly (line 48). In Node.js, Undici rejects with `fetch failed`. A `TypeError` with any other message stays a plain `TypeError`.

steps.title: The limit and the method come first
steps.say: `#calculateRetryDelay` is the retry decision. The PR keeps its first checks as they were: the retry limit, the method, and `shouldRetry`.

notes.text: `#calculateRetryDelay` returns the wait in ms before the next attempt, or it throws the error, which ends the retries. First, it throws when `#retryCount` has reached `retry.limit`.
By default, `retry.limit` is 2, so a request gets at most 3 attempts. `retry.methods` has no `post` and no `patch`.
Next, the method must be in `retry.methods`. A POST with a network failure throws here, now as a `NetworkError`.

A `shouldRetry` function still decides before the default checks. For a network failure, it now gets the `NetworkError`, not the raw `TypeError`. When it returns `undefined`, the default checks below decide.

steps.title: Only known error types get a retry
steps.say: After the first checks, the type of the error decides. Before, every error that no branch threw got a retry. Now only a `TimeoutError`, an `HTTPError` or a `NetworkError` can get one.

notes.text: Before, the timeout check could only throw. A `TimeoutError` with `retryOnTimeout` on fell through to the shared `return` at the end.
Now the timeout branch returns its own delay. `retryOnTimeout` is `false` by default, so a `TimeoutError` still throws.
The `HTTPError` branch also returns its own delay now. So each known type ends inside its own branch.
Before, every error that no branch threw reached this `return`. So even a bug in a custom `fetch` got 2 more attempts.
Now a last gate throws every error that is not a `NetworkError`. Only a `NetworkError` reaches `#calculateDelay` here.
`isNetworkError` checks `instanceof NetworkError`. Like the guards for `HTTPError` and `TimeoutError`, it also accepts any error with the `name` `NetworkError`.
`#calculateDelay` is the backoff. It calls `retry.delay` with the attempt number. The default is `0.3 * (2 ** (attemptCount - 1)) * 1000`, so the first retry waits 300 ms and the second waits 600 ms.

steps.title: Wait, run the hooks, try again
steps.say: `#retryFromError` waits, runs the `beforeRetry` hooks, and starts the next attempt. This code is the same, but the hooks now get the `NetworkError`.

notes.text: `#retryFromError` takes the delay from `#calculateRetryDelay`. It throws a `TimeoutError` when the time that is left of `timeout` cannot cover the wait. Otherwise it waits.
Then each `beforeRetry` hook gets the error. For a network failure, this is now the `NetworkError`, with `request` and `cause`. Before, the hooks got the raw `TypeError`.
`#retryCount` goes up, and `#retry` runs `#fetch` again. A second network failure takes the same path and waits 600 ms.

steps.title: Without the await
steps.question: A later change removes the `await` from `return await timeout(...)` in `#fetch`. A GET then fails with `TypeError: fetch failed`. What happens with the default options?

options.text: The raw `TypeError` skips the `catch`, fails the last gate, and goes to the app with no retry.
options.why: Without `await`, the `catch` of `#fetch` does not see the rejection, and the last gate throws every error that is not a `NetworkError`.

options.text: Nothing changes, because the `catch` still sees the rejection and wraps it.
options.why: A returned promise without `await` rejects after the function has left the `try` block.

options.text: The raw `TypeError` gets 2 retries, as it did before this PR.
options.why: Before this PR, unknown errors fell through to the backoff, but the new last gate now throws them.
`timeout` passes the fetch rejection to `reject` unchanged.

steps.title: The retries run out
steps.say: The server stays unreachable. After the third failed attempt, the app gets a `NetworkError` instead of the raw `TypeError`.

steps.title: Checks for TypeError stop matching
steps.say: Before, a network failure reached `catch` blocks and the `beforeRetry` and `beforeError` hooks as the raw `TypeError`. Now it arrives as a `NetworkError`. Code that checks the type, the name or the message of the old error stops matching. The PR text does not mark this as a breaking change.

notes.text: `#fetch` now catches the rejection of the fetch. When `isRawNetworkError` matches, it throws a new `NetworkError`. The original `TypeError` stays only in `cause`.

The name is now `NetworkError`, not `TypeError`. The message changes from a runtime text, such as `Failed to fetch`, to `Request failed due to a network error: GET <url>`. A check on `error instanceof TypeError` or on the old message now fails.
`beforeRetry` hooks get the wrapped error. In issue #545, the maintainer suggested a `beforeRetry` hook that throws when `isNetworkError` from the `is-network-error` package returns false.

This file is an inlined copy of that package. Its check requires `error.name === 'TypeError'`, so it returns false for the wrapped error. A hook from issue #545 then throws on the first failure, and the request gets no retry at all.

steps.title: Unrecognized errors no longer retry
steps.say: Before, the default logic retried every error that was not a timeout or an `HTTPError`. Now it retries only a `NetworkError`. A real network failure that `isRawNetworkError` does not recognize now fails on the first attempt.

notes.text: Before the PR, every error that got past the timeout and `HTTPError` checks reached `return this.#calculateDelay()`. Now only a `NetworkError` gets there. Every other error is thrown at once.

A match needs a `TypeError` with one of these exact messages, or one of the patterns below. A custom `fetch` option that rejects with its own error class never matches. For example, `node-fetch` may reject with a `FetchError`.
The readme names this gap and points to `shouldRetry`. Apps that use such a `fetch` lose their network retries without a warning until they add a `shouldRetry`.

steps.title: A drop during the body is not a NetworkError
steps.say: `#fetch` wraps only the errors that occur before the response headers arrive. A connection that drops while the body streams reaches the caller as a raw `TypeError`. Ky does not retry it, and the `beforeError` hooks do not see it. This was true before the PR, but the new docs promise more.

notes.text: The readme says that a network error during the request becomes a `NetworkError`, and that Ky retries it.
The `timeout` helper resolves when `fetch` resolves. That happens when the headers arrive, while the body can still be on the wire.
`.json()` and the other body helpers wait for `result`, then read the body. This read is outside `#retry`, outside the catch in `#fetch`, and outside the `beforeError` loop.

The list has `terminated` for undici in Node.js. Undici may use this message when the connection drops during the body. In Ky, that error usually comes from the body read above, so `#fetch` may never wrap it.

steps.title: CORS failures also become a NetworkError
steps.say: Browsers report a blocked request with the same `TypeError` as an offline one. So a CORS failure, or a request that a browser extension blocks, now arrives as a `NetworkError`. An app that shows an offline message for `isNetworkError` shows it for a configuration bug too.

notes.text: Chrome uses `Failed to fetch` for a refused connection and for a CORS failure. Firefox uses its `NetworkError when attempting to fetch resource.` text for both. This check cannot tell them apart.

The readme gives only a DNS failure, a refused connection and offline as examples. Ky also retries a CORS failure, which cannot succeed. With the default `retry.limit` of 2, a GET makes 3 requests and waits 0.3 s and 0.6 s before it fails. That cost was there before the PR.

steps.title: The guard matches any error named NetworkError
steps.say: `isNetworkError` also accepts an error by its `name`, for errors from another realm. Web IDL defines a `DOMException` with the name `NetworkError`, and such an error has no `request`. `isTimeoutError` has the same pattern with the `TimeoutError` of `AbortSignal.timeout()`, so the PR follows an existing design.

notes.text: Any object with `name === 'NetworkError'` passes, and TypeScript then types it as a Ky `NetworkError`. The example above this guard reads `error.request.url`, which throws on such a `DOMException`.
`isKyError` now calls `isNetworkError`. So it also reports that `DOMException` as a Ky error.
`#calculateRetryDelay` uses the same guard. A custom `fetch` that rejects with this `DOMException` may get retries as if Ky made the error.
